title: Trade, Credit, and the Changing Fortunes of Jewish Drohitchin
summary: The records describe livelihoods from commerce and craft to farming, alongside a cooperative bank and the importance of transport and regional connections.

editorialConnections.recordTitle: Savings and Loan Cooperative People's Bank

editorialContent:
## A town whose market reached beyond its streets

The memorial book remembers Drohitchin as a place where Jewish livelihoods depended on the surrounding countryside. Its account of the [Drohitchin Jewish community](/communities/drohiczyn/records/mention_ea295fe81894b5b0f5282a34) describes traders and peddlers moving between town and village, buying animals and farm produce from landowners and peasants, then selling goods locally or forwarding them to exporters. At fairs and market days, rural sellers brought grain, potatoes, livestock, eggs, wool, mushrooms and homespun linen. Jewish shops offered the practical goods they wanted in return: cloth, thread, salt, tools, kerosene, herring and household supplies.

This was more than a row of shops. It was an exchange system connecting farms, workshops and households across the district. The book recalls village peddlers carrying small goods in a sack, while brokers dealt in horses and cattle and merchants handled produce in larger quantities. Blacksmiths, shoemakers, tailors, bakers, carpenters and other artisans served the same local economy. Drohitchin had little industry: the book recalls two tanneries, a small oil press and a straw-goods factory, all modest enterprises. These details are the memorial book’s retrospective picture, not a census of every occupation or business. ([jewishgen.org](https://www.jewishgen.org/yizkor/drohichyn/dro025.html))

The regional setting helps explain why such a market mattered. The memorial book places the town in Polesia, on a road between Brest and Pinsk, and remembers the nearby Bug as a historical boundary. The wider record confirms that Drohitchin belonged to the Polish Polesie region between the world wars, while also distinguishing it from the better-known Drohiczyn in present-day Poland. The latter is a different place; its records and history must not be merged with those of this community. ([jewishgen.org](https://www.jewishgen.org/yizkor/Drohiczyn/Dro003e.html))

## From market trade to timber and leather

Some residents’ work extended well beyond the weekly market. The memorial book’s account of the Warshavsky brothers, Zusha and Tuvia David, follows a path from rural enterprise to larger-scale business. The brothers worked in lumber and held interests in forests and estates; in 1907 they moved to Drohitchin. The book says that in 1911 they bought Nachum Shevinsky’s leather factory and developed it into a business selling to distant parts of the country. Nachum Shevinsky, a leather merchant who later emigrated to America, is also remembered as the manager of his own tannery and as a founder of a Kobriner Hasidim prayer house. The book names his children Zalman, Sheine, Tsipe, Sarah and Rachel, but the supplied account does not establish what became of each of them. ([jewishgen.org](https://jewishgen.org/yizkor/Drohichyn/dro207.html))

The story of the factory also shows how exposed local commerce was to political upheaval. The book says the Warshavskys lost their property when German forces occupied the town in 1915: fires destroyed their houses and leather factory, and German authorities seized timber and remaining leather. The brothers resumed work after the war, but the book portrays business under Polish rule as more difficult. That testimony conveys how survivors understood the change; it should not be treated as a complete account of economic policy or of every local business. The [forestry and timber trade](research:Drohitchin's interwar timber trade) is one thread where estate, export and confiscation records could add detail.

The wider account of occupations fits the memorial book’s picture of a small-town economy, while adding scale. Yad Vashem’s entry for Drohitchin in Polesie describes a Jewish population of about 1,500 between the wars, roughly three-quarters of the town, and says most earned their living in crafts and trade, especially agricultural produce. It also notes that the town became a county seat in 1925, bringing a construction boom and improved conditions for artisans. This independent record supports the central importance of trade and skilled work, while making clear that the community included far more than shopkeepers alone. ([wwv.yadvashem.org](https://wwv.yadvashem.org/yv/he/research/ghettos_encyclopedia/ghetto_details.asp?cid=257))

## Credit as a communal institution

For a shopkeeper needing stock, an artisan facing a slow season, or a family short of cash in winter, access to credit could determine whether a business survived. The memorial book describes a Charity Fund that offered interest-free assistance, and a People’s Bank that made low-interest loans, including loans to businesses buying merchandise or repaying debts. Households and artisans, too, could borrow through the difficult winter months and repay when summer brought better trade. The account emphasizes that these institutions served Jews in town and nearby villages—not simply the most prosperous merchants. ([jewishgen.org](https://www.jewishgen.org/yizkor/Drohichyn/dro049.html))

The cooperative People’s Bank was founded in 1911. Its director, Zekharyah Shmid, embodied the overlap between work and communal service. The memorial book remembers him as a blacksmith who helped his father at the forge before becoming a community leader and bank manager. It credits him with roughly thirty years of work for the cooperative. Yet the same account gives conflicting versions of his death: one says he died naturally in 1939, another that he died under Soviet rule in 1940, and a third that the Germans killed him in 1942. The memorial book does not resolve the difference, so neither should this account. The bank’s [director and lending records](research:Zekharyah Shmid and Drohitchin bank records) might help establish more about the institution’s operations and leadership. ([jewishgen.org](https://jewishgen.org/yizkor/Drohichyn/dro207.html))

These local institutions formed part of a wider cooperative tradition. YIVO’s account of Pinsk, a regional center, describes Jewish participation in river transport and trade and places commercial activity within the broader economic life of Polesia. Pinsk is not Drohitchin, and its history cannot prove how the local bank functioned. It does, however, help situate the town’s reliance on trade, transport and mutual support within a regional economy rather than an isolated shtetl story. ([smtp.yivoencyclopedia.org](https://smtp.yivoencyclopedia.org/article/476?utm_source=openai))

## New borders, new controls

War and changing borders repeatedly altered what people could sell, where goods could go, and who controlled businesses. The memorial book recalls the transfer of a passenger station from Nagorie to Drohitchin under Polish rule, a change that suggests a shifting local transport landscape. But its account also stresses that trains alone did not sustain the market: village routes, fairs, wagon traffic and exporters were part of the same network. In the First World War, occupation and fire destroyed businesses; after the war, the book describes timber and leather enterprises struggling to recover.

A still sharper rupture came with Soviet rule in 1939. Yad Vashem’s entry for this Drohitchin describes private trade and crafts being gradually abolished, with shops closed or nationalized and cooperatives established. In June 1941, German occupation brought robbery, forced labor and the destruction of remaining freedom to work. By April 1942, Yad Vashem records two ghettos: one for workers with occupations the Germans considered necessary, and another for the rest. Labor was no longer an ordinary livelihood or a route to household independence; it was imposed under coercion, while property and economic choice were stripped away. ([wwv.yadvashem.org](https://wwv.yadvashem.org/yv/he/research/ghettos_encyclopedia/ghetto_details.asp?cid=257))

Care is needed because Yad Vashem’s encyclopedia also lists another Drohiczyn, in the Białystok district, with a different prewar population and a separate wartime history. The entry for the Polesie town—the community discussed here—places it in the Polesie district and describes a much larger prewar Jewish population. Those figures must not be combined. The difference is a reminder that place-name variants and similar spellings can conceal separate communities. ([wwv.yadvashem.org](https://wwv.yadvashem.org/yv/he/research/ghettos_encyclopedia/ghetto_details.asp?cid=258))

## Work remembered, community dispersed

The memorial book captures economic life through vivid particulars: a peddler’s sack, a crowded fair, the blacksmith’s forge, a tannery’s leather and the bank’s winter loans. Its testimony connects these activities to a social world in which merchants, craftspeople, farmers and lenders depended on one another. The independent record adds the changing political frame: county-town growth in the 1920s, Soviet control over private commerce, then forced labor and the destruction of the community under German occupation.

Displacement carried parts of this world elsewhere, though the memorial book’s surviving accounts cannot represent everyone who emigrated, fled, or died away from town. Nachum Shevinsky is remembered as an emigrant in America, and the book traces some Drohitchiners’ later communal life in Chicago. Its account of aid associations and remittances suggests that economic ties could persist after migration, even as the town’s own marketplace was dismantled. What cannot be recovered from these accounts alone is the full fate of every family or business. That absence is not evidence that no records exist; it marks the next work of research.
